issues.title: Use of delegation_chain term language uses delegating tasks as the core concept
issues.author: saisrungaram-ai

issues.title: action_subject: The specific entity this transaction acts on
issues.author: saisrungaram-ai
issues.body:
**Problem Statement**
A token says what action to perform but not on which specific entity — leaving every service to figure that out independently.

**Simple scenario**
A loan approval token says action: approveLoan. But there are 50 pending loans. Which one? The loan service has to look up whose loan this is, cross-reference the agent's session, and guess.
More importantly: for shared resources (a document multiple agents can access, a shared account), saying resource: approveloan doesnt justify. The token must say this specific loan, for this specific applicant.

**Proposed claim name**: action_subject
"tctx": {
  "action": "approveLoan",
  "action_subject": {
    "entity_type": "loan_application",
    "entity_id": "loan-8821",
    "entity_ref": "alex.turner@acme.com"
  }
}

**A2A examples:**
"entity_ref": "agent:financial-analyst-workload"
"entity_ref": "workload:fraud-detection-service-v2"
"entity_ref": "urn:dataset:fraud-training-v3"
"entity_ref": "urn:device:sensor-prod-042"

**Taxonomy:**
entity_type — what class of thing. 
entity_id — unique ID within that class. 
entity_ref — how to address or resolve it in the target system.

issues.title: trigger_type: What caused this action to happen
issues.author: saisrungaram-ai
issues.body:
**Problem Statement**
There is no claim to distinguish "a human explicitly asked for this" from "an agent decided this on its own."

**Proposed claim:**

"agentic_ctx": {
  "trigger_type": "delegated"
}

**Taxonomy for different scenarios**
Values for trigger_type:
delegated — the principal in the chain explicitly requested this action
autonomous — the acting agent decided this on its own
scheduled — a time-based trigger
event — an external signal (webhook, queue message)

Token is incomplete without it: Any policy that enforces "agent must not autonomously trigger high-risk actions" cannot be enforced from the token alone without this claim. Audit logs tell you what happened after the fact — trigger_type enables prevention at authorization time.

Behavioral analysis note: trigger_type: autonomous on a sensitive action (like fund transfer) is a direct input to intent and behavior analysis in decision logs. Log it alongside the authorization decision.

issues.title: principal and type : Mandatory in every token, human or A2A
issues.author: saisrungaram-ai
issues.body:
**Why mandatory for both human and A2A:**

Human flow: principal.type = human
A2A flow: principal.type = agent
Scheduled: principal.type = scheduled bot

**Proposed claim**

"principal": {
  "type": "user" 
}

**Taxonomy  values for type:**
type: user | agent | scheduled bot | event

The type alone changes the trust level and applicable policies. Without principal, a consuming service cannot distinguish a token that originated from a human supervisor versus one that originated from an unattended cron job — even if the delegation chain looks identical.

**Token is incomplete without it**: 
Authorization decisions that depend on the nature of the originating authority — which most enterprise policies do — cannot be made correctly without this.

issues.title: client : Mandatory in agentic_ctx
issues.author: saisrungaram-ai
issues.body:
**Problem Statement**
The same agent can be invoked through different interfaces — direct API, MCP tool, workflow engine — and each carries a different trust level, but the token looks identical.

**Simple Scenario**
Your AI assistant has access to your company's HR system.

1. You open the assistant and ask it directly → you trust this call completely
2. An MCP tool inside a third-party app invokes the same assistant → medium trust
3. An unknown webhook triggers the assistant → low trust, needs scrutiny

In all three cases, the agent identity is the same. The agent_type is the same. But how it was invoked determines the appropriate authorization level. Without client, the HR system cannot distinguish these three scenarios.

**Why mandatory, not optional:**
MCP is now a standard interface for agentic systems. The same resource server will receive calls from direct agents, MCP tools, and workflow engines simultaneously. Policies that say "MCP tool calls must be scoped to declared tool IDs" or "workflow engine calls require additional verification" cannot be enforced without knowing the client type.

**Proposed claim**

"agentic_ctx": {
  "client": {
    "type": "mcp_tool",
    "id": "mcp::approve-loan-tool"
  }
}

**Taxonomy for different client types:**

type: agent | mcp_tool | workflow_engine | code_executor | api_gateway

**Token is incomplete without it:** 
As MCP adoption grows, resource servers need to differentiate trust levels by invocation interface — not just by agent identity.

issues.title: Prior art for future revisions
issues.author: GoetzGW
issues.body:
Hi Ashay,

Bjørn Baunbæk and Götz Wehberg from the Gimel Foundation here. This is a constructive prior-art notification for any future revision of draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents (currently -03, January 2026).

The transaction-token shape your draft proposes - short-lived, context-bound tokens minted per agent action with explicit actor and principal claims - is architecturally closer to where the AI-agent-authorization category needs to land than long-lived bearer tokens are. The Gimel Foundation has published a body of open-core specifications on AI-agent authorization that overlaps with at least three specific surfaces in the transaction-tokens-for-agents design space, and we wanted to put the references on the public record for any future revision.

**Three concrete touch-points** (not necessarily limited to these):

1. Actor and principal claims as candidate PoA Credential mapping. The actor and principal claims in your draft directly correspond to the principal-agent model formalized in GiFo-RFC 0115 (Power-of-Attorney Credential Structure). RFC 0115 carries a richer mandate object — principal, agent, scope, delegation chain, expiry, narrowing rules — that the actor / principal pair could be mapped onto in a future companion document or revision, in cases where the calling context needs to carry not just "who is acting on whose behalf" but also "what mandate authorizes that act and to what scope".
2. Multi-hop scope narrowing — already specified in GiFo-RFC 0115 §3.7. Once transaction tokens chain across multiple agent hops (Agent A → Agent B → Resource), the scope-monotonicity question becomes load-bearing. RFC 0115 §3.7 specifies mandatory scope narrowing: a sub-agent's credential can only narrow, never broaden, the parent's scope, and this is enforced cryptographically rather than by IdP policy lookup. This is the surface the broader category also names variously as "secure agent-to-agent delegation" and "agent-to-agent authorization". When that work intersects transaction-tokens-for-agents in a future revision, RFC 0115 §3.7 is published prior art.
3. Runtime validation of extended / per-action OAuth tokens. The token shape your draft proposes — a short-lived OAuth token with extended claims (actor, principal, transaction-bound context) that the resource server validates per action rather than per session — is structurally an extended OAuth token in the sense formalized by GiFo-RFC 0111 (Extended OAuth Tokens, Summer 2025). 

Please note, this is patent-pending technology of Gimel Foundation.

**One request for a future revision** (or a companion document)
A Related Work / Informative Reference entry naming GiFo-RFC 0111 and GiFo-RFC 0115 as the closest published prior-art surfaces for the three touch-points above. 

**What this is currently not**
Not an infringement assertion against draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-03 or any successor.
Not a request to change the substantive normative content of the draft itself.
Not a contribution.

Specs are at https://github.com/Gimel-Foundation. 

Happy to provide section-level pointers or take a call.

Bjørn Baunbæk and Götz Wehberg, on behalf of Gimel Foundation

the renamed ``-araut-00`` was genuinely useful. We've read it carefully

Below is an updated touchpoint mapping. Touchpoints 1–3 carry forward
the substance of the original notification, refactored against your
new structure. Touchpoints 4–7 are additional surfaces in ``-araut-00``
for which the Foundation has published prior-art before 16 April 2026
that wasn't called out in the first issue (not limited to these):


Updated Touchpoint Mapping
==========================

- **Touchpoints 1–3** — carried over from the original notification.

- **Touchpoint 4 — Per-action runtime evaluation by the resource
  server.** The "validate per action, not per session" posture and the
  replacement-chain enforcement maps to GiFo-RFC 0117 (GAuth Power
  Enforcement Point, 8 April 2026), which formalises a 16-check
  pipeline operating at action time on a credential rather than a
  session — the runtime counterpart to your draft's wire-shape work.

- **Touchpoint 5 — Cross-trust-domain interoperability.** The
  architectural premise of base Transaction Tokens — that a token is
  minted in trust-domain A and validated in trust-domain B — is the
  surface specified by GiFo-RFC 0116 (GAuth Interoperability,
  8 April 2026) for the GAuth family.

- **Touchpoint 6 — Token issuance, replacement, and administrative
  surface.** The management-plane verbs implied by Txn-Token
  mint / replace / revoke map to GiFo-RFC 0118 (GAuth Management API

  ecosystems.** Production deployment of ``-araut-00`` will need SDK

issues.title: Proposal: delegation_ctx claim for delegation relationship context
issues.author: vadimlander-prog
issues.body:
# Proposal: `delegation_ctx` Claim for OAuth Transaction Tokens for Agents

**Author**: Vadim Lander, Broadcom Identity Security
**Target spec**: draft-araut-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-02

## Abstract

This proposal extends the OAuth Transaction Tokens for Agents specification with a new optional JWT claim called `delegation_ctx` that characterizes the delegation relationship between agents in a multi-agent chain. While `agentic_ctx` describes the agent and chain integrity, and `scope` defines permitted operations, neither captures the nature of how authority was transferred at each hop. `delegation_ctx` fills this gap as an orthogonal, composable authorization input.

## Problem Statement

The current spec provides claims that answer:
- **Who** is acting? (`act`, `agentic_ctx.current_actor`)
- **Who** started the chain? (`agentic_ctx.originator`)
- **How deep** is the chain? (`agentic_ctx.chain_metadata.hop_count`)
- **What** operations are permitted? (`scope`)

But it cannot express:
- Is this a supervisory delegation or an on-behalf-of delegation?
- Is the delegated agent constrained to read-only operations?
- What business context (PCI, international, booking) applies to this delegation hop?
- Should the resource server enforce delegation-style constraints server-side rather than trusting the agent to self-constrain?

These are policy-relevant distinctions that resource servers need for fine-grained authorization decisions.

## `delegation_ctx` Claim

The `delegation_ctx` claim is OPTIONAL on the Txn-Token. It provides a container for delegation-relationship metadata, wholly replaced at each hop.

### Structure

```json
{
  "delegation_ctx": {
    "delegator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "delegator_type": "agent",
    "type": "onBehalfOf",
    "style": "constrained",
    "tags": ["booking", "international"]
  }
}
```

### Fields

| Field | Category | Required | Mutability | Source |
|-------|----------|----------|------------|--------|
| `delegator` | Server-computed | REQUIRED | Replaced each hop | Incoming token's `agentic_ctx.current_actor` |
| `delegator_type` | Server-computed | REQUIRED | Replaced each hop | Agent Registry lookup on `delegator` |
| `type` | Delegator-provided | REQUIRED | Replaced each hop | Replacement request body, TTS-validated |
| `style` | Delegator-provided | OPTIONAL | Monotonically narrowed | Replacement request body, TTS-enforced |
| `tags` | Delegator-provided | OPTIONAL | Replaced each hop | Replacement request body, validated against allowlist |

### Field Definitions

**`delegator`** (String, REQUIRED): Identity of the entity that delegated authority for the current hop. The TTS populates this from the incoming Txn-Token's `agentic_ctx.current_actor`. At initial issuance (first hop), the TTS sets this from the `act.sub` if present, or from the authenticated `client_id` for autonomous flows.

**`delegator_type`** (String, REQUIRED): Whether the delegator is a `"principal"` (human user) or `"agent"`. The TTS resolves this via the Agent Registry — the same lookup it already performs to decide whether to populate `agentic_ctx`.

**`type`** (String, REQUIRED): Nature of the delegation. Defined values:
- `"supervisory"` — delegator oversees and coordinates the delegatee's work
- `"onBehalfOf"` — delegatee acts as a proxy for the delegator
- `"autonomous"` — delegatee operates independently within granted scope
- `"escalation"` — delegatee handles a task the delegator cannot perform

**`style`** (String, OPTIONAL): Constraint level on the delegation. Defined values in descending order of authority:
- `"full"` — no additional constraints beyond scope
- `"constrained"` — delegatee is limited to a defined subset of operations
- `"scoped"` — delegatee is limited to specific resources or contexts
- `"read-only"` — delegatee may only perform read operations

Subject to monotonic constraint narrowing (see TTS Validation Rules).

**`tags`** (Array of Strings, OPTIONAL): Business-context labels for the delegation hop. Examples: `["booking", "international", "pci"]`. Validated against a trust-domain allowlist. Tags MUST NOT contain PII.

## Replaced Per Hop, Not Accumulated

Unlike `req_wl` (which appends workload history), `delegation_ctx` is wholly replaced at each delegation hop. Authorization decisions are scoped to the current delegation relationship — a resource server needs to know "who delegated to the current actor and under what constraints," not the full delegation history.

Historical delegation context is available through out-of-band audit log queries, which provide richer context (timestamps, request metadata) than an accumulated token claim could.

## TTS Validation Rules

### At Initial Issuance

If the TTS identifies the caller as an agent (via Agent Registry lookup) and `delegation_ctx` is requested:
- `delegator`: Set from `act.sub` if present, otherwise from authenticated `client_id`
- `delegator_type`: `"principal"` if `act` is present (human delegated to agent), `"agent"` if autonomous and originating from another agent
- `type`, `style`, `tags`: Accepted from request, validated per rules below

### At Replacement

**Server-computed fields** — TTS populates; caller MUST NOT provide:
- `delegator`: Set to `agentic_ctx.current_actor` from the incoming Txn-Token
- `delegator_type`: Resolved via Agent Registry lookup on `delegator`

**Delegator-provided fields** — caller provides; TTS validates:
- `type`: MUST be a recognized value. TTS MAY reject values inconsistent with context (e.g., `"autonomous"` when `act` is present and `sub` represents a human principal).
- `style`: Subject to **monotonic constraint narrowing**. TTS MUST reject if the requested style is broader than the incoming token's `delegation_ctx.style`:
  ```
  full > constrained > scoped > read-only
  ```
  A delegator with `style: "constrained"` MUST NOT delegate with `style: "full"`. If the incoming token has no `delegation_ctx` (first hop), no style constraint applies.
- `tags`: Validated against a trust-domain allowlist. TTS MAY enforce that delegated tags are a subset of the delegator's tags (monotonic narrowing).

### Rejection Conditions

TTS MUST reject the replacement request if:
- Request body contains server-computed fields (`delegator`, `delegator_type`)
- `style` violates monotonic narrowing
- `tags` contain values not in the trust-domain allowlist
- `type` is not a recognized value

## Integration with Agent Registry

The -02 draft states the TTS SHOULD have access to an Agent Registry. `delegation_ctx` leverages this same registry:
- `delegator_type` is resolved via the Agent Registry (same lookup the TTS already performs to decide whether to populate `agentic_ctx`)
- `style` narrowing validation MAY use registry-defined maximum delegation authority per agent
- `tags` allowlists MAY be maintained in the registry alongside agent metadata

No parallel infrastructure is introduced.

## Wire Format

### Replacement Request Body

```json
{
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange",
  "subject_token": "<existing-txn-token>",
  "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:txn_token",
  "delegation_ctx": {
    "type": "onBehalfOf",
    "style": "constrained",
    "tags": ["booking", "international"]
  }
}
```

Only delegator-provided fields appear in the request body. Server-computed fields (`delegator`, `delegator_type`) in the request body MUST cause rejection.

## Effective Authorization Model

The effective authorization at any hop is the intersection of three independent dimensions:

- **`scope`** limits **what operations** are permitted (attenuate-only, TTS-enforced per -02 spec)
- **`delegation_ctx.style`** limits **how those operations may be exercised** (monotonically narrowed)
- **`delegation_ctx.tags`** provide **business context** for policy evaluation

No single claim can unilaterally escalate beyond what the others permit.

## Example: Three-Hop Travel Booking Chain

```
User (alice@example.com)
  -> Orchestrator Agent (supervisory, full, hop_count=1)
    -> Travel Agent (onBehalfOf, constrained, hop_count=2)
      -> Flight Booking Agent (onBehalfOf, read-only, hop_count=3)
```

### Hop 1 — Orchestrator Agent

```json
{
  "sub": "user:alice@example.com",
  "act": { "sub": "orchestrator-agent-v2" },
  "scope": "travel.book travel.read travel.cancel",
  "agentic_ctx": {
    "current_actor": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "originator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "chain_metadata": { "hop_count": 1 }
  },
  "delegation_ctx": {
    "delegator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "delegator_type": "principal",
    "type": "supervisory",
    "style": "full",
    "tags": ["travel"]
  }
}
```

### Hop 2 — Travel Agent

```json
{
  "sub": "user:alice@example.com",
  "act": { "sub": "orchestrator-agent-v2" },
  "scope": "travel.book travel.read",
  "agentic_ctx": {
    "current_actor": "travel-agent-v3",
    "originator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "chain_metadata": { "hop_count": 2 }
  },
  "delegation_ctx": {
    "delegator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "delegator_type": "agent",
    "type": "onBehalfOf",
    "style": "constrained",
    "tags": ["travel", "booking"]
  }
}
```

### Hop 3 — Flight Booking Agent

```json
{
  "sub": "user:alice@example.com",
  "act": { "sub": "orchestrator-agent-v2" },
  "scope": "travel.read",
  "req_wl": "apigateway.trust-domain.example,orchestrator-v2.trust-domain.example,travel-agent.trust-domain.example",
  "agentic_ctx": {
    "current_actor": "flight-booking-agent-v1",
    "originator": "orchestrator-agent-v2",
    "chain_metadata": {
      "hop_count": 3,
      "min_assurance_level": "medium"
    }
  },
  "delegation_ctx": {
    "delegator": "travel-agent-v3",
    "delegator_type": "agent",
    "type": "onBehalfOf",
    "style": "read-only",
    "tags": ["flights", "international", "pci"]
  }
}
```

At hop 3, `scope` is attenuated to `travel.read` and `delegation_ctx.style` is `read-only`. Even if the flight booking agent has broader capabilities registered in the Agent Registry, the effective authorization is constrained by both dimensions independently.

Reading this token, a resource server knows:
- **Who**: alice (`sub`), acting through orchestrator-agent-v2 (`act`)
- **Chain**: 3 hops deep, medium assurance, currently flight-booking-agent-v1
- **Delegation**: travel-agent-v3 delegated on-behalf-of with read-only constraint, tagged for flights/international/PCI context
- **Scope**: attenuated to `travel.read` only

## Security Considerations

**Server-computed fields prevent chain position misrepresentation.** Agents cannot claim to be delegated by an entity other than the actual previous `current_actor`. The TTS is the sole authority for `delegator` and `delegator_type`.

**Monotonic constraint narrowing prevents privilege escalation.** A delegatee cannot receive broader `style` authority than the delegator holds. This mirrors the -02 draft's monotonic attenuation of `min_assurance_level`.

**Tags are validated against trust-domain allowlists.** This prevents injection of arbitrary labels that could influence policy evaluation. Tags MUST NOT contain PII to prevent data leakage through token propagation.

**Historical delegation contexts require out-of-band audit.** Since `delegation_ctx` is replaced per hop, intermediate delegation states are not preserved in the token. Deployments requiring delegation history SHOULD maintain audit logs at the TTS.

## Broader Applicability

`delegation_ctx` is applicable beyond Transaction Tokens:
- **RFC 8693 Token Exchange**: `delegation_ctx` can be included in exchanged access tokens to characterize the delegation
- **AuthZEN evaluation requests**: `delegation_ctx` can be passed as a subject or resource property in PDP evaluation calls

This positions it as a general-purpose delegation characterization mechanism for the agentic identity ecosystem.

## Complete Context Model

The full authorization context with `delegation_ctx` answers distinct questions:

| Claim | Question |
|-------|----------|
| `sub` | For whom? |
| `act` | Who is the original actor? |
| `agentic_ctx.current_actor` | Who is acting now? |
| `agentic_ctx.originator` | Who started the chain? |
| `agentic_ctx.chain_metadata` | How deep and how trusted is the chain? |
| `delegation_ctx` | How was authority transferred at this hop? |
| `scope` | What operations are permitted? |
| `tctx` | What is being done? |

To start with, I'd request to take a look at latest https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-araut-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-02.html and if required edit the proposal. The latest one has clear definitions of what 'act' is, and what first and last agents are in the chain , along with hop count. The server computed values does make sense as they are authoritative. I will take a deeper look.

In general, delegation is being relooked at https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/authorization-problem-we-keep-half-solving-george-fletcher-hueee/ and there's been discussions around this.

One important aspect to note is also that, any information added to Txn token flows all the way in service call chain graph including agentic and non-agentic workloads so we have think about where do these policies apply? At what point in the graph? Can we apply some of them during access token issuance as part of delegation checks and so we don't really need to transport all the context deep down about delegations?
